title: Local planning: Task automation differs from employment change
desc: Separates occupational forecasts from automated tasks and emphasizes geographically uneven lawyer growth, training and recruitment needs.

kps.k: Employers anticipate workforce reconfiguration through both automation and augmentation, not a single path of job replacement.
kps.d: The Future of Jobs Report 2025 draws on the World Economic Forum’s 2024 employer survey to describe intentions for 2025–2030: 85% plan upskilling, 73% accelerated automation, 70% recruitment for new skills, 63% technological augmentation and 51% redeployment into growing roles. Alongside these measures, 41% plan reductions where skills or roles become less relevant. The substantive tension is between investment in workers and selective contraction; these strategies can coexist. The supplied evidence records employer expectations rather than observed AI-caused employment effects or disagreement between independent sources.

kps.k: AI collaboration creates substantial anticipated training and recruitment needs, but employers do not expect every worker to make the transition.
kps.d: The report’s global AI-strategy benchmarks show 77% planning to train existing workers to work alongside AI, 69% to recruit AI-tool design skills and 62% to recruit people skilled in AI collaboration. Across the broader transformation outlook, employers expect 29% of workers to receive training within their current role, 19% to train and redeploy, and 11% to be unlikely to upskill; 41% would need no training. These forecasts make workforce development central without establishing that planned training will succeed or prevent displacement.

kps.k: Task automation and occupational employment projections measure different changes and should not be conflated.
kps.d: Employers project predominantly human task execution falling from 48% to 33% by 2030, predominantly technological execution rising from 22% to 34%, and combined execution rising from 30% to 33%. These task shares are not job-loss rates. Occupational forecasts separately show uneven growth and contraction: information and technology services anticipates 132% net growth in software and applications developers and a 30% decline in data-entry clerks, while infrastructure expects growth in assembly work and civil engineering. The report also tracks demographic, economic, climate and geopolitical drivers, so its overall employment projections cannot be attributed to AI alone.

kps.k: The legal-sector contribution is a forecast of modest, geographically uneven lawyer growth, not evidence of law-firm displacement.
kps.d: The report’s lawyer rows give global net growth of 2%, compared with −4% in Central Asia, +6% in South-eastern Asia and +8% in Hong Kong SAR. The broader professional-services profile anticipates upskilling at 88% of employers, recruitment for new skills at 75% and technological augmentation at 70%. It also places AI and big data alongside enduring analytical, creative and interpersonal skills. These figures inform legal workforce planning, but the professional-services category does not isolate law firms, and the lawyer projections do not establish AI’s causal employment impact.

kps.k: Variation and implementation barriers make local workforce planning more informative than a uniform automation forecast.
kps.d: Automation intentions differ between high-income economies (77%) and lower-middle-income economies (57%), while larger companies anticipate greater AI-driven business-model transformation. Employers identify labour-market skill gaps (63%) and organisational culture or resistance to change (46%) as barriers. They see potential in training provision and funding, education reform, promotion pathways and other talent measures. The practical implication is to assess skills, redeployment capacity and organisational constraints alongside technology adoption; the survey does not demonstrate that respondents’ preferred interventions work.

vlens.an: The market-analyst/consultancy evidence supplied supports the proposition that task automation should not be equated with employment decline and that workforce planning must account for local variation. The Future of Jobs Report 2025 presents automation, augmentation, upskilling, recruitment, redeployment and selective staff reductions as concurrent employer intentions rather than a uniform replacement trajectory. It also distinguishes changes in how tasks are performed from occupational forecasts and treats AI as one of several drivers of workforce change. Its legal contribution is consistent with the proposition’s emphasis on uneven outcomes: projected lawyer growth is modest globally but varies across regions, while professional services anticipates substantial upskilling, recruitment and technological augmentation. Material variation appears by geography, sector and employer size, including different automation intentions, AI exposure, training needs and lawyer-growth forecasts. These findings remain expectations reported by surveyed employers for 2025–2030, not observed AI-caused employment effects; the professional-services data also do not isolate law firms. Because the supplied evidence comes from one report, this assessment characterises that source rather than market analysts, consultancies or the press generally.

elens.an: The 2025 source supports the proposition that task automation should not be equated with employment change. The Future of Jobs Report 2025 presents automation, augmentation, upskilling, recruitment, redeployment and selective staff reductions as concurrent employer intentions for 2025–2030, rather than as a uniform path from AI adoption to job loss. It also supports localised planning: automation intentions, training requirements and occupational projections vary materially by geography, sector and organisation size. Within legal work specifically, the report projects modest global lawyer growth but divergent regional outcomes, including contraction in Central Asia and growth in South-eastern Asia and Hong Kong SAR. Material qualifications are that these are surveyed employers’ expectations, not observed AI-caused effects; task shares are not headcount measures; professional services does not isolate law firms; and AI is only one of several transformation drivers. Because the evidence comes from one report, its repeated regional and industry profiles represent internal variation within that source, not independent corroboration or a measure of wider prevalence.

parents.t: Employer workforce planning: Skills and organisational capacity mediate AI’s employment effects
